A style that focuses on retaining possession and winning the ball back quickly. Looks to play out of defence and and create chances through patient, short-passing build-up play.
Gegenpressing relies on every player in the team working hard and, above all else, being fit and mobile enough to press the opposition immediately after losing the ball.
Tiki-Taka aims to dominate the match through a combination of intense pressing and a very patient, short-passing attacking approach. A more extreme variant of the Control Possession style.

Vertical Tiki-Taka aims to dominate the match through a combination of intense pressing and a very patient, short-passing attacking approach. The team is instructed to play narrow in attack, congesting the pitch but also creating smaller passing distances between teammates to allow for quick one-twos and fluid attacking play.
Wing Play looks to get into high-quality crossing positions as much as possible. Players are expected to make regular overlapping runs in order to overload the flanks in attack.

Route One aims to get the ball into the opposition half as quickly as possible. Not wanting to risk giving the ball away near their own box, the team will instead play long passes into attacking teammates to start attacks.
Looks to draw the opposition out to leave them vulnerable on the break. Players will be expressive on the counter, looking to combine with eachother and play through the opposition to create chances.

Looks to draw the opposition out to leave them vulnerable on the break. Players will look to get the ball forward as quickly as possible on the counter in order to create chances against an unsettled defence.

A defence-focused style that primarily looks to deny the opposition goalscoring opportunities. Traditionally uses an Out of Possession formation with 3 centre-backs to provide extra cover and stability in the backline.

A defence-first approach that primarily looks to restrict the amount of attacking opportunities the opposition are able to create. Ceding the majority of possession, the team looks to take advantage of counter-attacks and set pieces to score goals.
This mentality is intended for situations where the team needs to shut up shop, usually reserved for desperate situations during the final minutes of a match.
This mentality is best employed for matches where the opposition are heavy favourites to win, or in situations where the team need to start taking less risks in order to help see out the game.

This mentality is a good starting strategy for matches in which you believe the opposition are the stronger team, but you still feel you can break with some regularity. In possession, the team will take slightly fewer risks with the ball, playing with a slightly lower level of tempo and urgency. However they will still commit numbers to counter-attacking opportunities when they arise. Out of possession, team will play a slightly deeper defensive line in order to absorb pressure.

This mentality is an ideal starting strategy for matches against similar-strength opponents, or situations where you want a careful balance between risk and reward. In possession, the team will play with a balanced level of tempo and urgency, not trying to force the issue but also still looking to create attacking opportunities where possible. Out of possession, the team will play a balanced defensive line depth.
This mentality is best employed for matches in which you believe you are the stronger team but are wary of your opponent’s counter-attacking threat.
This mentality is best employed for matches where the team are heavy favourites to win, or in situations where the team need to start taking more risks in order to find a goal.
This mentality is intended for situations where the team needs to go for broke to try and score a goal, usually reserved for desperate situations during the final minutes of a match.

The Overlapping Centre-Back combines the responsibilities of a Centre-Back and a Winger, looking to provide protection to the team during early phases of attack, while also getting into crossing positions by making overlapping runs in the final third of the pitch.

The Full-Back is a key player in modern football, having to supplement their traditional defensive duties with overlapping runs down the wing to support forward play and help attacks overload the final third.

A defensive midfielder who looks to drop into their team's defensive line as they progress the ball up the pitch, the Half-Back acts as an additional central defender.

A situation when the ball is not in play, e.g. when play has not been restarted after the ball has gone out of bounds or a foul has been committed. It also applies before each kick-off, either at the start of each half or after a goal has been scored. In a dead ball situation, players can position the ball with their hands prior to restarting play. Furthermore, even though the ball is not in play, the referee may still issue yellow or red cards for any incident that occurs off the ball. Fouls, on the other hand, can occur only while the ball is in play.
Dead balls are situations in a match when the ball is not in play.

The colloquial name given to the most senior team of a football club. There are relatively few restrictions as to who can be in the first team squad, though these can differ by nation or league rules. Some members of the first team squad who either don't meet the required standards, have had a long-term injury, or who are unhappy are sometimes demoted to the fm_pedia#1 or fm_pedia#2. Naturally, the aim of almost every player in either of the squads below the first team is to be promoted to it and feature in matches. The most promising reserve youth players might remain playing in the youth squad, but also train with the first team in order to be exposed to a more senior level of football.
The first team squad are a club's top team. The aim of almost every player at a club is to be a part of it.

The main role of a goalkeeper is to prevent the opposition from scoring goals. Some shots or passes that come their way travel too quickly, or are judged to be travelling too quickly, are instead hit back with their hands or other body parts (often legs) back into play, usually in a different direction to the initial shot or pass. There's always a risk that the rebound will be followed up by an opposition player for a clearer scoring opportunity. An advanced metric that attempts to quantify the act of pressing in football. OPPDA focuses only on actions in the area of the pitch in which the opposition team might reasonably execute a high press, which is calculated to be decided on three-fifths (or 60%) of the pitch nearest to the other team’s goal. In this area, the number of passes made by the opposition is divided by the number of defensive actions made by the out-of-possession team to give a number for OPPDA.These defensive actions are tackles, interceptions, challenges (or failed tackle attempts), and fouls. The number that this calculation produces gives a value to the intensity of the out-of-possession team’s press. A low OPPDA value indicates a higher intensity to a team’s pressing.
OPPDA calculates how many actions the opposition performs in the three-fifths of the pitch nearest to the other team's goal before possession changes hands.

Each FIFA Member association has men's and women's teams from youth level through to the most senior level. World Cups take place once every four years, with qualification and possible participation for them scheduled in the calendar alongside or adjacent to qualification and possible participation at other tournaments and officially sanctioned matches.If a player is called up to represent their national team, it is considered a huge honour to have the opportunity play for them, regardless of its world ranking at any given time.

National teams are considered the highest level of football at every stage of a player's career. They follow a match or competition schedule designed to have matches alongside or adjacent to domestic club competiitons.

Every player who is considered actively fm_pedia#1 to be fm_pedia#2 for a national team is included in a database for the national team manager and their staff to keep tabs on. When players retire from international duty or from playing altogether, they are removed from the pool.
A National Pool is a database of players eligible to be called up for a national team.

FIFA set the criteria for which players are eligible for national teams in officially sanctioned tournaments and matches. Generally, a player needs to be tied to a certain nation and have a demonstable 'clear connection' to it in order to be considered eligible to play for them, though this is complicated in particular instances; for example, the United Kingdom has four separate countries (England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland) with separate member associations.
Eligibility is whether a player can be called up to a certain national team. In some instances, players are eligible to play for multiple national teams.

When matches are coming up in the calendar, eligible players in the National Pool are chosen by the national team manager to make up a squad, normally consisting of 23 players or more. If the players haven't already been contacted, they often find out through official announcements made on broadcast or social media to inform them they have been 'called up'.
Call-Ups is the term given to players who are chosen by their national team managers to be in squads for friendlies or competitive matches.

International matches (especially tournaments) have deadlines prior to beginning for national team managers to finalise their squads, after which they can only be changed in minor ways under very specific circumsances, such as a player suffering a long-term injury. Once that hard deadline has passed, even another long-term injury to a player cannot result in a fm_pedia#1 taking their place.
The Final Squad Selection is the final list of players a national team manager can choose prior to the start of matches taking place, especially tournaments.

When squads are selected for international matches, there are sometimes changes to them right up to and even past the deadlines. These can take place because of injuries that would rule players out of the upcoming series of matches; if the matches are taking place partway through a club season, players often withdraw for a number of reasons, including if they are carrying a knock or are otherwise not fully fit. The national team manager usually has a list of backups to hand to cover such eventualities.
Withdrawls, Backups, & Replacements describe the changes in a national team squad prior to matches or tournaments taking place.

In 2004, a new ruling came into effect that permitted players to represent one national team at youth level and a different one at senior level. This was further amended in 2020, where a rule change was approved to allow players to switch national teams three years later if they have played no more than three competitive matches at senior level prior to them turning 21, including no appearances in FIFA World Cup matches or continental finals (e.g. the UEFA European Championship).
Switching National Teams is possible for players to do under specific circumstances, such as having played no senior level international matches after turning 21.

Through a number of different circumstances, players can be eligible for more than one national team, including where they were born, the nationalities of their biological parents and/or grandparents, or where they have moved to ('naturalised') during their lives. Whilst recognised dual nationality status is not uniform globally, in football, it gives players of sufficient ability more choices as to which national team to represent.National team managers can often try to persuade such players to represent the one they're in control of, or they can choose for themselves. This choice can also be influenced by the likelihood of one national team regularly fm_pedia#1 for major international tournaments.
Dual Nationalities refers to players being eligible for more than one national team, such as when they hold two passports for different nations.

With the exception of a tournament's host nation(s), every other national team has to successfully go through at least one stage in order to participate at that tournament. The qualification process varies wildly from confederation to confederation and tournament to tournament; for example, some national teams have to almost immediately start their qualification process for the next FIFA World Cup after the previous one has just ended, whereas others might not start for another two years.
With the exception of host nations for a tournament, every other national team must play a number of matches and sometimes more than stage of matches in order to qualify.

In order for both the qualification process and tournaments themselves to run smoothly, governing bodies hold public events called draws to ensure they are conducted fairly and openly. There are usually other considerations (such as geography and seedings) to take into account. For example, if there are multiple host nations for a tournament, it is almost certain that those host nations will play their initial games 'at home'.
Draws are impartial processes that determine which teams play which, and at what stages of a competition these matches take place.

fm_pedia#1 for both the qualification for a tournament and the tournament itself that has at least one group stage, which is a way of dividing the participants into smaller sections (mini-leagues) of their own, often before a knockout stage to determine the overall winners. Depending on the rules and tie-breaker criteria, the number and identity of national teams that progress from those groups varies from competition to competition.
Tournament Groups are 'mini-leagues' of teams in a tournament who play each other in order to determine which one of them qualifies for the next stage.

It may be necessary to have an additional qualification stage after the (final) group one for an international tournament. If the spaces for one confederation's national teams at a tournament is a certain number, but the participants were drawn into a number of groups in the final stage that is not neatly divisible into a smaller number (16 spaces for 10 groups of five national teams in each group, for example), then a play-off stage or stages are held to fill the remaining spaces.

International Play-Offs are an additional stage, usually after the main section(s) of qualification for a tournament, which are held in order to determine the last few participating national teams for that tournament.

At the end of a group stage, some teams can finish level on points with each other. Different criteria are used in differing orders to determine which in those situations advance to the next stage. These tie-breakers include: goal difference (goals scored minus goals conceded), goals scored, the head-to-head record between the teams on the same number of points, and the number of yellow or red cards received. If all of these remain level, then lots are drawn to ultimately determine the victors.
Tie-Breaker Criteria & Order are the ways different competitions separate teams which have finished level on points in order to determine which of them qualify for the next stage of a tournament.

As more and more nations have become member associations of fm_pedia#1, the number of spaces both in qualification for tournaments and the tournaments themselves has similarly expanded to ensure a fair representation and opportunities to qualify. At the first FIFA Men's World Cup in 1930, 13 national teams from three confederations competed.Gradually, the number of teams grew until almost a century on from the inaugural tournament, 48 teams from all six confederations will compete in 2026, with the fm_pedia#2 now guaranteed at least one space for the first time.
Historical Expansions refers to more national teams becoming FIFA member associations, and the tournaments expanding in order to accommodate them.

As the game of football has grown, tournaments have been created to help drive further interest, with interest often peaking during the tournaments themselves. Alongside the FIFA World Cup, each confederation has at least one international tournament considered to be 'major' for both men's and women's football; these tournaments are considered major because of a number of factors, including their relative rarity in the football calendar (none of them are ever held more frequently than biennially, for example).More often than not, the top level(s) of the domestic club calendar comes to a complete stop during the tournaments in order for the players to freely participate, and for more people to watch them compete.
Major International Tournaments are highlights of the football calendar when they occur, which is usually at most once every two years.
Stadia Selection Crtieria refers to the requirements the competition organisers have in place in order to choose which stadia will be used during a tournament.

FIFA employs a vast array of different criteria in order for a stadium to be considered eligible, which are sorted into five different categories, with the 'top' category being the most stringent one only normally seen at elite level. The 'bottom' category is the equivalent of grassroots level. In order for an existing or a planned stadium to be considered for the men's or women's World Cup, it has to be in the 'top' category in every aspecta. These criteria consist of, but are not limited to: at least 40,000 seats; a roof covering all the seating areas; ample parking spaces; at least 1,000 hospitality seats and 20 boxes; 0.5% of the total capacity to be given over to wheelchair spaces, and two giant screens.There have historically been many stadia that have been built for a major tournament, and the criteria are designed to ensure that these continue to be well used long after the tournament has finished (if it doesn't play host to regular club matches). The only other consideration taken into account is a geographical spread of stadia in the host country or countries; a hard cap of three stadia per city is usually employed, though in practice, there is rarely more than one stadium in a city that would meet all of the 'top' category criteria. Most other major tournaments will employ a mixture of the first two categories.
Host Selection Criteria refers to the requirements potential host nations need to have in place in order to be seriously considered as candidates to stage a tournament.

Hosts need to prove they have the existing infrastructure to be considered for major tournaments. This includes transport in and of host cities, suitable training camps, and enough stadia of the required standard to ensure the tournament goes smoothly. Historical expansions of many major tournaments have made it more difficult for one host nation to manage it by itself, with the burden being shared between two or three.With the FIFA World Cup, there is a policy to rotate which confederation hosts tournaments in order to prevent one dominating.

National teams and clubs sometimes use gaps in the football calendar to locate their squad and key staff away from their usual 'homes' in order to work more intensively on aspects of their game from a tactical and technical perspective, and to also have fewer distractions. These training camps also sometimes operate in a location with a vastly different climate to the one they're used to, either in preparation for a tournament or to maximise the effects of training in a limited timeframe.When national teams are still involved in tournaments, they tend to stay secluded in the training camps for the duration of their stay, except when travelling to and from matches.
Training Camps are used by national teams and clubs to intensely work on aspects of their game, often either in gaps in the calendar or before and during a tournament.

Standing for Fédération Internationale de Football Association, but far more commonly and simply known as FIFA, it is the self-regulatory governing body of world football, founded in 1904 to oversee international competition between a handful of national member associations. Its membership has since swollen to 211 across six confederations.FIFA has several objectives in its organisational statutes, which include growing football internationally, ensuring the sport is accessible to everyone, and advocating for integrity and fair play. It also organises major international football tournaments, most notably and famously including the Men's World Cup and Women's World Cup for national teams, and the Men's Club World Cup and Women's Club World Cup for clubs across the globe.All FIFA competitions generate sponsorship money, some of which goes towards meeting its objectives. It is led by a president elected by the national member associations, and they are supported by vice-presidents from each of the six confederations.
FIFA is the governing body of world football, which also organises competitions such as the Men's and Women's World Cups.

The footballing embodiment of continents, confederations have national associations as members, grouped by geography with a few exceptions. The confederations oversee and support the development of the game from the most senior national team level down to the grassroots, and are in turn supported by FIFA in several ways, including financially.
Confederations are the footballing equivalent of continents, with each body looking after the development of the game in the areas they govern.

The Union of European Football Associations, UEFA is the governing body for football in Europe, it holds major international competitions such as the Men's European Championship and Women's European Championship for national teams on a quadrennial basis, and club competitions such as the UEFA Champions League, Europa League, Conference League, and the Super Cup on an annual basis.
UEFA is the governing body for football in Europe, and it runs competitions such as the Men's and Women's European Championship.

The Asian Football Confederation is the governing body for football in Asia. It holds major international competitions such as the Men's Asian Cup and Women's Asian Cup for national teams on a quadrennial basis, and club competitions such as the AFC Champions League on an annual basis.
AFC is the governing body for football in Asia, and it runs competitions such as the Men's and Women's Asian Cup.

The Confederation of African Football is the governing body for football in Africa. It holds major international competitions such as the Men's African Cup of Nations and Women's African Cup of Nations for national teams on a biennial basis, and club competitions such as the CAF Champions League on an annual basis.
CAF is the governing body for football in Africa, and it runs competitions such as the Men's and Women's African Cup of Nations.
CONCACAF is the governing body for football in North America, Central America, and the Caribbean. It runs competitions such as the Men's and Women's Gold Cup.

The Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football is the governing body for football in North America, Central America, and the Caribbean. It holds major international competitions such as the Men's Gold Cup and Women's Gold Cup for national teams on a biennial basis, and club competitions such as the CONCACAF Champions Cup on an annual basis.
CONMEBOL is the governing body for football in South America, and it runs competitions such as the Copa América and Copa América Femenina.

Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol, known more commonly by the acronym CONMEBOL, is the governing body for football in South America. It holds major international competitions such as the Men's Copa América and Copa América Femenina for national teams (typically between once every two years to once every four years), and club competitions such as the Copa Libertadores on an annual basis.
OFC is the governing body for football in Oceania, and it runs competitions such as the OFC Men's and Women's Nations Cup.

The Oceania Football Confederation is the governing body for football in Oceania. It holds major international competitions such as the OFC Men's Nations Cup and OFC Women's Nations Cup for national teams on a quadrennial basis and once every three to four years respectively, and club competitions such as the OFC Champions League on an annual basis.
